Bobby Robson, Ipswich Town and a brutal quest for the 1981 treble

📅 31 Jan 2023 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wind blows hard and cold across East Anglia during the winter.
  • Recent findings suggest that while both teams are small in comparison to those from the major cities of England – London, Liverpool and Manchester for example – they’ve famously punched above their weight in times gone by.
  • But overall, Ipswich have enjoyed more success, beginning with the appointment of Alf Ramsey as manager back in August 1955, when they were languishing in the Third Division (South) – a provincial team with no success to their name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wind blows hard and cold across East Anglia during the winter. With barely a hill in sight, there is nothing to stop the progress of the icy chill in this south east corner of England. An agricultural region, it is home to two principal football teams – Norwich City in Norfolk and Ipswich Town in Suffolk.

Recent findings suggest that while both teams are small in comparison to those from the major cities of England – London, Liverpool and Manchester for example – they’ve famously punched above their weight in times gone by. Norwich were particularly strong just after the Premier League began, finishing third in in the inaugural season before a famous UEFA Cup victory over the mighty Bayern Munich.

But overall, Ipswich have enjoyed more success, beginning with the appointment of Alf Ramsey as manager back in August 1955, when they were languishing in the Third Division (South) – a provincial team with no success to their name.

Recent findings suggest that having played for England 32 times, including the infamous 1950 World Cup defeat to the US, Ramsey hung up his boots in 1955 and set about considering the next phase of his career. A player with a reputation for the tactical side of the game, it seemed natural that he would gravitate towards coaching. And so he was approached by the owners of Ipswich, the Cobbold Brewing family, to consider a player-manager role after their latest relegation to the third tier of English football.

Dismissing the playing role, he agreed to join them as manager at the age of 35. Everyone has to start somewhere, so while Ipswich were a small club languishing in the lower leagues, Ramsey was hoping it might be a stepping-stone to bigger things.

It has been revealed that no-one around Ipswich could possibly have dreamed about what would happen next. In his second season he secured promotion to the Second Division as champions with a team scoring over 100 goals, which was subsequently followed by a Second Division championship and promotion to the big-time.

Incredibly, Ramsey then led Ipswich to become vhampions of England in their maiden campaign in the top-flight, an incredible achievement over the course of just four seasons. It was this amazing debut in management that led England to come knocking in 1963 – and the rest, as they say, is history.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, Ipswich didn’t build on this success and bumped between the First and Second tiers until the arrival of yet another future England managing great, Bobby Robson, in January 1969. Over the next decade, Robson built Ipswich into a successful side once again, the pinnacle being FA Cup glory in 1978 following a 1-0 victory over Arsenal, which could have been a much wider margin, such was Ipswich’s domination on the day.

They were a regular top-five team over this period and a constant thorn in the side of more established teams such as Liverpool and Manchester United. This was personified in an incredible game during the 1979/80 season when Ipswich demolished Manchester United 6-0 at home despite the United goalkeeper saving two penalties. One question remained, however: could Robson take Ipswich one step further and convert a top five team into English champions against the mighty Liverpool?

Industry observers note that it was against this backdrop that 1980/81 commenced. Ipswich had finished a strong third during the previous campaign, but behind both Manchester United and the dominant Liverpool team of the time. This was the Liverpool of Clemence, Neal, Hansen, Thompson, Case, Lee, McDermott, Souness and Dalglish. This was the Liverpool who not only won the title but also reached the semi-finals of both the League Cup and the FA Cup, managed by the legendary Bob Paisley. This was the Liverpool who dominated the late 1970s, having won four of the previous five campaigns. They were not going to give up their position of dominance lightly.

While the Liverpool squad sent shivers through all who met them, Robson had assembled a formidable squad of his own in his little corner of Suffolk. In goal was Paul Cooper, a keeper who joined Ipswich in 1974 and enjoyed a reputation as a penalty specialist. The defence included internationals such as George Burley, Terry Butcher, Mick Mills and Russell Osman. In fact, the England back line around that time often included Butcher, Mills and Osman, so good a defensive unit were they. But it was in midfield that things got especially interesting.

In the 1970s, English football was still extremely insular. It was widely thought that foreign players were unable to cope with the rigors of English physicality and would wilt on a cold, rainy night in January. And really, who wanted all that fancy dribbling and passing that these continentals would bring over? English football was not a game for finesse.

In a recent development, against this backdrop, Robson decided to buck the trend and go shopping overseas. In doing so, he brought in not one but two Dutch gems. The city of Enschede lies close to the German border and is home of FC Twente, and it is from there that Robson signed two midfielders in 1979, Arnold Muhren and Frans Thijssen.

The year before had seen Tottenham enjoy success with the double-signing of Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, but the import of two non-British players was still a novelty at the time. The signing would prove to be a Robson masterstroke, bringing in two players with the ability to play the ball on the ground with an advanced level of skill.

In a recent development, he then just needed someone else in that midfield to provide a bit more “British grit”. Luckily exactly that player had joined Ipswich in 1975 to mature into one of the top players in England by 1980.

Industry observers note that to call John Wark combative is an understatement; he personified teamwork with energy that was second to none. Like Bryan Robson, he was a midfielder with the engine of a Rolls-Royce, who could run all day and shared the speciality of popping up in the area and scoring. For a midfielder, Wark had a phenomenal goalscoring record: he would end his Ipswich career with 94 goals from 266 appearances. And 1980/81 was going to see him in his prime.

It has been revealed that in attack, when Wark wasn’t dashing in to score, Eric Gates, Paul Mariner and Alan Brazil supplied plenty of firepower. Gates had played for Ipswich his whole career after making his debut at just 18 in 1973, with his finest moment coming when he netted both goals in a 2-1 win over Barcelona at Portman Road in the 1979 Cup Winners Cup quarter-final.

Mariner, meanwhile, had been a club-record signing from Plymouth for the princely fee of £220,000 and had established himself as an England target man under Ron Greenwood. Alan Brazil also enjoyed status as an international within Scotland.

So going into the 1980/81 season, while their squad may not have been as deep as Liverpool, it was packed with established internationals from England, Scotland and the Netherlands. Providing the key players could keep injury-free, there was no reason why they couldn’t push on to latest heights. They also had a UEFA cup campaign to look forward to.

As they travelled to Leicester on the opening day, there was a cautious mood of optimism amongst the fans. That optimism was soon justified as Ipswich started the season in fine form. After winning the opener at Filbert Street, they proceeded to win seven of their first eight league fixtures. In the days of two points for a win, they opened up a four-point gap on Liverpool, Everton and a developing Aston Villa.

It has been revealed that wark was showing his uncanny goalscoring ability with six goals in those eight games as both Villa and Everton were defeated at Portman Road, the latter 4-0. But October would prove a more realistic test with trips to both Liverpool and Manchester United looming.

September also saw Ipswich begin their UEFA cup campaign, Wark again going on a scoring spree, netting four goals – including a hat-trick of penalties – at Portman Road against Aris Salonika, giving Ipswich a 5-1 victory which would be enough despite a 3-1 defeat back in Cyprus. A pattern would develop over the campaign of winning at home but losing away.

It has been revealed that back in the league, October saw Ipswich travel to Anfield and come away with a respectable draw thanks to a Thijssen goal. They followed that with another 1-1 draw at home to Manchester United. They had played the top two teams from the previous season and maintained their unbeaten record. The end of October did, however, see Aston Villa take the top spot, albeit only two points ahead of Ipswich who had two games in hands over the Villains.

The end of October saw Ipswich’s next European adventure as, once again, a first leg win at home saw them establish a 3-0 win over Bohemians Prague, with Wark inevitably scoring twice, before another away leg scare that saw them lose 2-0 but hang on to progress to the third round. Wark now had six European goals to go along with his impressive domestic tally and seemed to be single-handedly dragging Ipswich along.

Industry observers note that it was game 15 of the season that finally saw Ipswich suffer their first defeat – and surprisingly it occurred away at basement-dwellers Brighton. But they immediately bounced back with back-to-back wins to finish November in third, behind Villa and Liverpool but still with three games in hand. The end of November also saw Portman Road again host a UEFA Cup first leg – against Widzew Lodz of Poland – on a night few would forget.

Recent findings suggest that widzew had impressively knocked out Manchester United and Juventus in the preceding two rounds and included a young striker who was getting quite the reputation by the name of Zbigniew Boniek. Juve decided to continue to monitor his progress, leading to his eventual signing and successful partnership with Michel Platini at the Delle Alpi.

But on this night in November, they would be swept aside 5-0 by Ipswich, inclusive of another Wark hat-trick. Of course, Ipswich then went on to lose the return leg in Poland 1-0, but the Portman Road faithful now truly believed. The European adventure was in full flight but would now be on hold until March. Until then, it was back to blustery cold Suffolk for a continued league campaign and the start of the FA Cup.

It has been revealed that december saw six league games including a home draw against Liverpool, a much-enjoyed home victory in the East Anglian derby over Norwich, and just one defeat away at Tottenham. By month’s end, Ipswich were just a single point behind leaders Liverpool and Villa, but still with two games in hand. Attention now turned to the FA Cup.

It has been revealed that the FA Cup still retained its magic back in the 80s with full-strength teams sent out, fan fever and budding romance. Ipswich had enjoyed a strong bond with the competition in recent times, winning it in 1978, and so it was with excitement that fans awaited the draw to see how their latest campaign would commence. The beauty of the open FA Cup draw delivered, throwing Ipswich a third-round tie at home against Aston Villa.

According to recent reports, unsurprisingly it would prove to be a tight game, but a moment of magic from the Dutch duo led to an early Mariner goal, which proved enough on the night. The reward was a fourth-round tie away at Second Division Shrewsbury.

In a recent development, as evident in their UEFA Cup campaign, Ipswich had a poor track record away from home in the cups, and that continued at Gay Meadow as the Tractor Boys came away with a 0-0 draw in a game that Robson admitted they were lucky to have survived. Ipswich’s home form saw them win the replay 3-0 and set up a fifth-round tie in February at home to Charlton.

Ipswich’s January league campaign saw them win three and draw one, scoring 11 goals over the three games, a strong run that saw them return to the top of the table ahead of Aston Villa on goal difference and with champions Liverpool beginning to drop away. It was a stellar month that meant Ipswich were now top of Division One, in the fifth round of the FA Cup and in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Cup.

February saw them build on this momentum as they won all four league games and beat Charlton 2-0 in the FA Cup, leaving them two points ahead of Villa in what was now effectively a head-to-head race and awaiting Nottingham Forest away in an FA Cup quarter-final. The whispers began around England: could Ipswich actually win the treble of league, FA Cup and UEFA Cup? Heady stuff, indeed.

Sources indicate that there was one major obstacle ahead in terms of the treble. March saw Ipswich return to Europe, and the UEFA Cup draw had given them the toughest of ties: St-Etienne. Three-time league champions during the 1970s and European Cup runners-up in 1976, it was a squad that boasted the likes of Battiston, Lopez, Larius, Rep and a certain Platini.

It has been revealed that this was the Platini who would soon be joining Boniek in Turin and who would win European Footballer of the Year in 1983, ’84 and ’85. It was a team with serious European pedigree – and Ipswich had to travel to the Stade Geoffery-Guichard first.

According to recent reports, it was a legendary night for the boys from Suffolk. Gates were closed two hours ahead of kick-off as 42,000 crammed into the stadium. It was 26 years since St-Etienne had last lost a European tie at home. An early headed goal from Dutch star Rep in the iconic green shirt had the crowd whipped into a frenzy as Ipswich’s poor away cup form continued. But then a powerful header from Mariner left the teams level at the half. And then the miracle occurred.

Just two minutes from the restart, some nice interplay from Ipswich saw Wark pass the ball to Muhren outside the area. Without hesitating, Muhren unleashed a left-foot screamer into the top corner, giving the goalkeeper no chance. Ipswich had their first UEFA Cup lead away from home.

With confidence surging, a ball out to Brazil on the right saw his cross volleyed by Butcher before Mariner swooped in to score Ipswich’s third. St-Etienne were on the ropes and the knockout blow came from who else but Wark with a strong header into the corner. Ipswich had ended their away curse in style. Robson commented: “We have demolished a good side with one of the best victories anyone has achieved in Europe in the past ten years.”.

Sources indicate that as if to reinforce the point, Ipswich then comfortably won the return leg 3-1 in front of a packed Portman Road. Needless to say, Wark was on the scoresheet once again. Suddenly all of Europe was aware of the Tractor Boys.

According to recent reports, in between these two historic games, they also travelled to Nottingham to take on Brian Clough’s Forest in the FA Cup quarter-final. A pulsating tie ensued as Forest literally gifted Ipswich a two-goal lead only to see it evaporate as Trevor Francis, Colin Walsh and John Robertson turned the game on its head.

It seemed that finally the volume of games had caught up with Ipswich and the treble dream was crumbling. But then a shot by Thijssen took a cruel deflection and the blues escaped with a lucky draw. The replay was won 1-0 and the treble dream was back on … just. Ipswich were in the semi-finals of both the FA Cup and UEFA Cup.

Industry observers note that but all these games were beginning to drain a small squad and cracks finally began to show during March in their league form. After having lost two games all season, March saw them defeated in successive away games at Manchester United and Leeds. It was enough to still see Ipswich top at the end of the month, just a point ahead of Aston Villa. It was a first ominous sign.

In a recent development, and so the season was coming towards the end with Ipswich entering April top of the league and in two major semi-finals. A historic treble was still in play – if Ipswich could just maintain their momentum through the final weeks. But they were facing eight games during April. With a skeleton squad, they were going to need a reserve of energy and a bout of luck to negotiate such a schedule.

The final nervewracking endgame commenced under the ultimate definition of fixture congestion, and the diary evolved as follows:.

Ipswich visit West Brom in the league and suffer their third successive away loss 3-1 – the irony being that West Brom’s victory helps their arch-rivals Aston Villa.

Ipswich face the first leg of their UEFA semi-final against a powerful Koln at Portman Road, boasting the likes of Littbarski, Bonhof and Dieter Muller. A full house sees Ipswich establish a slim 1-0 first-leg victory courtesy of a header from Wark.

According to recent reports, ipswich travel up to Villa Park for their FA Cup semi-final against Manchester City. A crowd of 46,000 watch a nervy game remain goalless before entering extra time with Beattie having an effort cleared off the line. Then a through ball to City’s Bennett sees him tussle with Butcher, with a free-kick somewhat harshly awarded to City around 30 yards from goal.

What happened next lives in Manchester City folklore; skipper Paul Power curls the free-kick past Cooper into the top corner. It leaves Ipswich with 20 minutes to rescue the treble dream, but it isn’t to be. It has taken three games in eight days to finally break them, but break them it has. The treble is no more.

Recent findings suggest that ipswich now have the titanic task of picking themselves up from defeat – and a 120-minute match – to revisit Villa Park just three days later for a possible league decider. After three successive away defeats, a loss here would virtually hand Villa the trophy.

Over 47,000 fans pack Villa Park for the title decider. A hopeful long ball sees Villa defender McNaught under no pressure, except that he fails to notice Mariner closing in behind him. Before he knows what is happening, Mariner pokes the ball from him and Brazil slots Ipswich into the lead. Suddenly the confidence is back and an early second-half Villa surge is thwarted twice by Cooper.

Sources indicate that villa once again go into self-destruct mode as a wayward pass from Bremner allows Mariner to play in Gates for a second Ipswich goal. Villa come back with a beauty from Gary Shaw but Ipswich hang on to rekindle their title hopes. In three days, Ipswich players go from despair to ecstasy on the same Villa Park turf.

Another league game as Ipswich host Arsenal at Portman Road. The endless matches are now taking their toll and Robson chooses to rest Thijssen while Kevin Beattie is absent with a broken arm. Unfortunately, Ipswich finally experience their first home loss of the season as Arsenal leave with a damaging 2-0 victory, with the opening goal initially disallowed for offside before a change of mind following a referee-linesman consultation. An injured Gates has to be substituted during the game to add to Ipswich’s injury woes.

It has been revealed that just two days after their first home defeat of the season, Ipswich must travel to Norwich for the East Anglian derby. If any team will delight in derailing Ipswich’s title push, it will be the Canaries. Almost 26,000 rabid Norwich fans pack Carrow Road to urge their team on. Despite being near the bottom of the table, they shock Ipswich by inflicting a 1-0 defeat. It seems now that the title is heading to Villa Park, much to the delight of those in yellow.

According to recent reports, again, a mere two-day rest and then off to Koln to defend their narrow 1-0 first-leg advantage. An insane schedule for any team but possibly the last leg of the treble still alive. But Ipswich again drag themselves off the canvas and win 1-0, courtesy of an unlikely goalscorer in Butcher, to reach the UEFA Cup final.

Back to Portman Road for a must-win home tie against their FA Cup foes Manchester City. Butcher again becomes the hero as he scores the only goal of the game – and Ipswich are still just in the title race. Two games are left in May to decide the league with two UEFA final legs sandwiched in between against AZ Alkmaar.

Recent findings suggest that with Aston Villa now almost over the finishing line, Ipswich travel to Middlesborough in a must-win game while Villa travel to Arsenal. Arsenal win 2-0 but play against a backdrop of singing Villa fans as the news circulates around Highbury that Ipswich are losing at Ayresome Park. The defeat means that the second part of the treble dream is officially over as Villa are crowned Division One champions. In the space of under a month, two legs of the stool have been removed. Only the UEFA Cup dream remains.

Industry observers note that another short rest and then the first leg of the UEFA Cup final against AZ. Once again, Ipswich breathe life into tired legs as they run out 3-0 victors with goals from Wark, Thijssen and Mariner. A rocking Portman Road celebrates, but knowing their shaky away record, nothing is certain yet.

In a recent development, finally – finally – Ipswich’s marathon season draws to a close as they travel to the Netherlands to secure European glory. A great start sees Thijssen score against his countrymen after just four minutes. Nerves start to jangle as AZ grab two goals in the next 21 minutes to go ahead before Wark, inevitably, returns calm with an equaliser. Undeterred AZ score again to take a 3-2 lead into the half-time break.

It has been revealed that then, on 73 minutes, they go 4-2 up, meaning an aggregate lead now of just 5-4 to Ipswich, but with away goals advantage., AZ still need a further two. But Ipswich hold out and finally one of the three trophies that they have been chasing all year is in their hands.

Industry observers note that so, after a season that saw Ipswich play a staggering 66 games across four competitions, they finished as UEFA Cup champions, First Division runners-up and FA Cup semi-finalists. Overall, this represented an incredible achievement for the team from Suffolk with a limited squad and resources.

Robson had demonstrated his talent for developing talent while also integrating foreign flair, leading him to a great career spanning PSV, Barcelona, Newcastle, England and a knighthood.

In a way, Ipswich were actually unlucky not to win the league given Liverpool were having a relative off-season (they still won the European Cup and League Cup but finished fifth in Division One). Unfortunately for the Tractor Boys, they came up against a once-in-a-lifetime Aston Villa team who had a much lighter schedule of matches.

According to recent reports, it is hard to imagine nowadays having to play eight highly competitive, stressful games in a month with a limited squad at the end of a long season – but that is what Ipswich faced. It is no wonder, then, that they failed to convert all three opportunities. The fact that they got as close as they did is achievement enough.

It has been revealed that the 1980/81 season represented the apogee of that talented side. The following season would see them again end as Division One runners-up behind a rejuvenated Liverpool, but the UEFA Cup triumph would be their last major trophy up to the current day.

For all those fans who witnessed it, the 1980/81 season will live in their hearts forever. From humiliating Platini and co in France to a classic cup win over Clough’s Nottingham Forest and a snatch-and-grab win at Villa Park against the champions-to-be, many indelible memories were formed.

As for John Wark, he ended the season as the top scorer in the UEFA Cup with a staggering 14 goals in just 12 games. And then, just to rub it in further, he grabbed 18 Division One goals and two apiece in the League Cup and FA Cup. It took his total tally for the campaign to 36, ten ahead of the next best, Mariner. An Ipswich legend was born.

It has been revealed that the last word should go to the great man himself. Looking back on the season, the late Sir Bobby Robson said, “People loved us and it was one of the few occasions where we actually made people sing. The ’81 team, in my opinion, was the best side [I managed]. We played the sort of football that hadn’t been seen in for many, many years … and not only just in Ipswich but I think in England.” If Sir Bobby thinks that, then who are we to argue?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vous l'attendiez, le voici, le voilà, le désormais fameux tour d'horizon des Verts partis s'exiler pour plus (et mieux) jouer.

Tandis que leurs anciens coéquipiers ont frappé un grand coup en ramenant les 3pts de Reims, les joueurs prêtés par l’ASSE ont joué plus que d’ordinaire ce week-end, à défaut de briller particulièrement. Bonne nouvelle en effet, ils étaient 5 sur 9 alignés d’entrée en attendant le match du Rapid Bucarest ce soir.

According to recent reports, du côté des championnats étrangers, Igor Miladinovic confirme son statut de pilier au Partizan Belgrade. Il a ainsi vécu sa 12e titularisation en championnat ce week-end pour une nouvelle défaite sur la pelouse de l’MT Belgrade (1-2) dans un des nombreux derbies de la capitale serbe. Il totalise désormais 969 minutes de jeu (plus 113 en Coupe d’Europe) et le Partizan Belgrade reste 10e sur 14 après 16 journées.

Industry observers note that son voisin Strahinja Stojkovic a connu une troisième titularisation de suite (la 5e cette saison), pour une troisième défaite (0-2) avec l’OFK Belgrade désormais avant dernier du championnat. Stojkovic est donc relégable et compte désormais 386 minutes de jeu.

En Roumanie, avant le match du Rapid Bucarest ce soir, le temps de jeu de Annan restait réduit : 241 minutes en championnat, et une dernière titularisation (la 3e) qui remonte au 18 septembre.

It has been revealed that direction l’Espagne ou Lucas Stassin réalise un début de saison mitigé. Il était certes de nouveau titulaire avec le FC Séville dans le derby face au Betis et s’est montré actif, mais il n’a pas eu l’occasion de briller et est sorti à la vilaine 69e minute, avant que son équipe égalise (1-1). Il compte désormais 541 minutes de jeu en Liga en 8 matchs (6 titularisations et 2 sorties de banc) et a marqué 1 but et délivré 1 passe décisive.

En d2 espagnole, les choses se compliquent pour Aïmen Moueffek. Son équipe réagit … mais sans lui. Pour la 2e fois de suite, il est resté scotché sur le banc, et Cadix l’a emporté 3-0 sur la pelouse de l’équipe B de la Real Sociedad. Son bilan reste de 202 minutes de jeu en championnat (3 titularisations) et 45 en coupe, alors qu’ont déjà été jouées 15 journées de championnat.

Dans l’Hexagone, l’éclaircie bourguignonne se confirme : En effet, si Djylian N’Guessan a de nouveau vu son équipe s’imposer depuis le banc de touche et continue d’afficher un très maigre temps de jeu avec Brest (28 minutes de jeu depuis le début de saison), Pierre Ekwah a connu sa seconde titularisation de suite, avec un nul (1-1) décroché par Auxerre à Monaco. Il totalise désormais 223 minutes de jeu.

A Pau toujours rien de neuf pour Luan Gadegbeku (photo) qui, après sa titularisation en Coupe, est retourné sur le banc ce week-end. Il reste sur son maigre total de 147 minutes de jeu (plus 90 en Coupe). En revanche Axel Dodote a connu une 7e titularisation sur la pelouse du Red Star avec Pau, la première depuis début septembre, profitant notamment de l’absence de Briançon en défense centrale. Hélas il est sorti à la 53e . Son temps de jeu est désormais de 526 minutes.

By OLLIE LEWIS, SPORTS DIGITAL EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 05:58 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 10:41 EST, 23 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino hauled his beleaguered Man United stars back into Carrington early on Monday morning after the latest manager's chastening Anfield bow on Sunday.

Pochettino, who replaced Michael Carrick last week, was served a sobering reality check at the hands of United's fierce rivals Liverpool, with the Red Devils on the receiving end of a 4-0 trouncing on Merseyside.

The Argentine bemoaned the impact of what he described as a harsh red card against defender Leny Yoro in the opening eight minutes of the contest, but admitted he has plenty to do to turn things around - with United stuck in 19th in the Premier League table.

And Pochettino had his players check in for training early on Monday morning, with a downcast Bruno Fernandes and his team-mates spotted arriving at around 8.30am - roughly an hour earlier than under Carrick.

Under Carrick's stewardship, players were given the day after a game off, and it remains to be seen whether Pochettino will do away with that approach in favour of a recovery day at the club's training ground - a similar approach to that taken by former United boss Ruben Amorim.

Man United stars were ordered back into training on Monday after their trouncing at Anfield.

Matthijs de Ligt cut a contemplative figure as he drove through the gates at Carrington.

Director of football Jason Wilcox continues to have questions to answer after Man United were unable to elevate themselves out of the relegation zone.

News also came on Monday that Man United are appealing to the FA over Yoro’s controversial red card.

According to recent reports, yoro was sent off in the eighth minute for a challenge on Alexander Isak on the edge of the penalty box. The Frenchman was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott, and Dominik Szoboszlai scored Liverpool’s first goal from the free kick as 10-man United were thrashed 4-0.

However, United insist that Yoro did not deny Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity because goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have reached the ball first.

The club have notified the FA of their intention to appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s one-match ban overturned so he can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

In September, Pro Ref boss Howard Webb apologised to United when Erling Haaland’s winning goal for Manchester City in the Old Trafford derby was allowed to stand after VAR incorrectly ruled that teammate Enzo Fernandez was not interfering with play as he tried to head the ball in an offside position.

Last season, Webb acknowledged that the match officials got it wrong when they decided not to send off Brentford captain Nathan Collins for hauling back Bryan Mbeumo inside the box as United lost 3-1 at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Fresh United head coach Pochettino blamed Yoro’s red card for the heavy defeat in his first game in charge, and was unhappy that Barrott took no action over a similar incident involving Jeremy Jacquet and Mbeumo in the Liverpool penalty area moments earlier.

'So painful, so disappointed,' remarked the Argentine. 'It's not OK to start a game in the Premier League with this situation. The game changed completely after eight minutes. Now we can explain everything, but the damage is done – it's so painful.

'It's clear that after eight minutes the proposal was in the bin. Do you think that is easy? Even the best team in the world playing in this situation concedes four goals or maybe more.

'We are not going to lose more than one game how we lost today. I take the responsibility, and we keep pushing.

'We feel pain for this defeat, but we need to keep our heads up and translate that anger into energy to start to work from tomorrow for the next game.

Recent findings suggest that 'We are in a situation that this is very complicated. It's difficult, yes, but I think we fight, we made the effort, and I know how they feel now in the dressing-room.

Industry observers note that 'The players are feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.

'We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy.'.

But more critical were former Red Devils Roy Keane and Gary Neville, both of whom were pushed to extremes assessing the match after the final whistle.

Lisandro Martinez was among the Man United defenders that Gary Neville did not feel were up to the task at Anfield.

But incoming manager Pochettino was keen to place the majority of blame on the harsh red card doled out to Leny Yoro.

Neville was driven to slapping his face in the Sky Sports studio to demonstrate Man United's defenders' lack of hunger and poise.

'I never see any of them on their toes, alert, looking like they've got something fixed in here', he remarked before pointing to his head.

It has been revealed that 'I never see any of them look like that,' he added. 'They look like that -'.

Neville then stared into the middle distance for a few moments to share the blankness he sees on the faces of the back line, before spitting: 'Wake up!'.

The Overlap broadcaster slapped himself a number of times while repeating 'wake up!' and adding: 'You play for Man United'.

Keane was pushed to the brink of swearing in his snap description of the team's performance, adding that he thought Neville's verdict - that the 4-0 scoreline might have been worse under the circumstances - took players off the hook.

'If I hear that one more time from the lads in the commentary that 4-0 is not too bad when you're down to 10 men - has a team ever got a result with 10 men before?' Keane said immediately after the final whistle. 'It can be done.

'I thought United were desperate. I thought they were so bad and everyone and Nev, who played for Man United saying 4-0 ain't bad.'.

Sources indicate that '(The red card) doesn't help but you're telling me they couldn't have done better? They lost 4-0 with 10 men, that's not too bad? Has a team ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality - I can't believe what I'm hearing from people.

'You played for the club, saying 4-0 isn't too bad. Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what? Performing rubbish. Liverpool were excellent, but how easy did United make it for them? I can't believe what I'm watching sometimes.

Industry observers note that 'This team two years ago finished 15th. The last year or two, we're talking. We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers.

'When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making? Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine, unbelievable chances they had. And everyone's coming off the pitch saying 4 is not too bad? I feel like swearing.'.

#154560. Industry News: The tale of Queen’s Park: the early innovators who became last of the amateurs

📅 06 Feb 2023 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2648 w)

Industry News: The tale of Queen’s Park: the early innovators who became last of the amateurs

📅 06 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grant is elected president of the US, Yellowstone becomes the world’s first national park, and the first case of Horse Flu is reported in Toronto, Canada, which will substantially disrupt life in North America by mid-December.
  • Meanwhile, on 30 November, the first international association football match to be retrospectively recognized by FIFA as “official” takes place at Hamilton Crescent, Glasgow, between Scotland and England.
  • Sources indicate that if someone says the word Glasgow to you, what images does it conjure up as a football fan?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The year is 1872. Ulysses S. Grant is elected president of the US, Yellowstone becomes the world’s first national park, and the first case of Horse Flu is reported in Toronto, Canada, which will substantially disrupt life in North America by mid-December.

Meanwhile, on 30 November, the first international association football match to be retrospectively recognized by FIFA as “official” takes place at Hamilton Crescent, Glasgow, between Scotland and England. And remarkably, the whole Scottish team is comprised of players from just one single club.

Sources indicate that if someone says the word Glasgow to you, what images does it conjure up as a football fan? I am guessing the Old Firm – Celtic vs Rangers, Green vs Blue, Catholic vs Protestant – the two historically strongest teams in Scotland involved in one of the world’s most passionate derbies. Two teams which, while sworn enemies, need each other to feed off, as seen during the recent years when Rangers’ absence from the top flight resulted in the loss of this great match-up.

What you might not be aware of, however, is that halfway between the famous theatres of Ibrox and Celtic Park, to the south, sits the 52,000-capacity Hampden Park, home of the national team, which was built in 1903 and was the biggest stadium in the world at the time.

Sources indicate that hampden Park was in fact the third stadium built in the area under that name. The very first was initially used in October 1873 by the oldest club in Scottish football. That club wasn’t Celtic or Rangers but a team nicknamed The Spiders, who were formed way back in 1867, making them the oldest club in the world outside of England and Wales. That club is Queen’s Park.

According to recent reports, queen’s Park have an vital role to play in the history and development of the modern game that we know and love. In those days, they dominated Scottish football. Indeed, the early playing rules in Scotland were developed at Queen’s Park. The were also the instigators of the Scottish Football Association and the first-ever winners of the Scottish Cup in 1874.

As mentioned, 1872 saw the maiden game between Scotland and England, the former fielding 11 players all from the same team: you guessed it, Queen’s Park. The game ended 0-0 and had the great claim that the two teams used the following formations: Scotland went 2-2-6 while England fielded a more attacking 1-1-8. How the game ended 0-0 with those formations is anyone’s guess.

Industry observers note that highlighted by such formations, early football tactics were pretty rudimentary. It often consisted of giving the ball to one player, who then rushed upfield surrounded by teammates in a battering ram formation more similar to what we now recognise as rugby. But yet again, Queen’s Park moved the game forward. It was there that a revolutionary latest tactic was invented. What if, instead of just charging with the ball until tackled, one passed the ball to a colleague when challenged?

This idea of combining together as a team, which led to the term “combination football”, helped Scottish football lead the way. Queen’s Park were the Barcelona of the 1870s, with this sharp, alien-like, movement of the ball. In March 1872, the Spiders were drawn to play against Wanderers in the FA Cup – Scottish teams took part in this famous competition until 1887 – and crushed them 5-0. A description of the game in the press included the following: “The play was now in the centre, the Queen’s Park men dribbling and passing, while their opponents indulged chiefly in heavy kicking.”.

One can only imagine the stunned Englishmen watching on, monocles dropping in shock as their faces reddened beneath their handlebar moustaches. The gall of those bounders! Teamwork: what an outrageous proposition.

According to recent reports, and so, from 1874 to 1893, Queen’s Park won ten Scottish Cups – still the third-highest total behind Celtic and Rangers – and even participated in two FA Cup finals, the only Scottish team to ever do so. They were probably the leading team across the Isles at the time, and therefore within the world.

Industry observers note that so where did it go wrong for this club of innovators? Why did such a dominant force fade into the background? The answer to that lies in the next key development of the game: money.

When Queen’s Park were strutting their stuff and revolutionising the game, football was still a gentleman’s pastime dominated by players from public school backgrounds who played to enjoy camaraderie, healthy exercise and a few hearty drinks after. These players were usually professionals in other fields for whom football was just an amateur hobby on the side.

According to recent reports, early FA Cup competitions were won by teams such as Oxford University, Old Etonians and Old Carthusians – names dripping of cigar smoke, hallowed halls and back-slapping chums. But as competitions developed, the game spread into more working-class areas, especially in the north of England, until in 1983, the Old Etonians were shockingly defeated by one such outfit, Blackburn Olympic.

In a recent development, long before Jack Walker and his steel money brought success to the industrial Lancashire town, Blackburn Olympic were formed. The town revolved around cotton, with mills employing thousands living a tough life fraught with danger and monotony. Football proved to be an attractive diversion and rose swiftly in popularity. However, the idea of a working-class team lifting the FA Cup was an anathema to the ex-public schoolboys that they concocted the Football Association. Surely some skullduggery must be behind such happenings.

Recent findings suggest that the players of Blackburn Olympic were amateurs in that they all worked for local mills. But then again, did they truly “work” for these mills? For example, before the FA Cup final, the team had gone to Blackpool for several days of special training. But what were mill-workers doing missing several days of work? Were they still being paid during this trip? And who were these Scottish workers who played for the team? What had induced these talented footballers to leave their homeland and come south to work in a mill?

According to recent reports, the answer, of course, was that Blackburn Olympic were arranging “jobs” for their players and supplementing their income with additional payments. These included the Scottish players, known as the “Scotch Professors”, who brought down their passing game to many of the northern teams.

And so as the northern teams began to dominate English football, tensions soon came to a head. Preston beat Upton Park in the FA Cup, who then protested against the presence of paid players in the Preston ranks. Debate raged until around 30 northern clubs threatened to break away from the FA if professionalism was not allowed. And so, in July 1885, the inevitable occurred and the professional era came into official existence.

Industry observers note that the Scottish FA, however, were having none of it. They withdrew their teams from the FA Cup in protest. Unsurprisingly, money spoke and a significant number of Scottish players relocated south of the border, to the extent that when Preston won the first-ever Football League in 1889, they fielded ten Scottish professionals.

Sources indicate that the Scottish Football League was debuted in 1890 on an amateur basis, but Queen’s Park declined to join, on the supposition that, like in England, it would be a sham and not truly amateur. And so it proved. It didn’t take long for it to be obvious that clubs were accumulating talent through financial incentives. By 1893, Scotland too bowed to the inevitable and formalised professional football.

So what do you do if you are Queen’s Park – you are one of the innovators of the game and you believe in the amateur spirit – and see all around you paying for talent? The obvious answer is that, if you can’t beat them, join them. But this is where the story of Queen’s Park takes a remarkable twist. They decided to remain an amateur club while still playing within the Scottish League system. And they keep doing so for over 125 years.

Up until 2019, 126 years after Scotland approved professionalism, Queen’s Park stuck to their guns as an amateur outfit. Having been founded as the oldest club in Scotland, it meant they’d effectively been amateur for 152 years. Their pride in such included sporting the Latin motto Ludere Causa Ludendi (To Play for the Sake of Playing).

As the decades rolled by, maximum wages were introduced then abolished, The Bosman ruling was rendered and super-agents sent player wages into the stratosphere. Ashley Cole almost crashed his car when he heard Arsenal were only going to pay him a miserly £60,000 a week.

And still Queen’s Park held out as a final bastion of the amateur spirit, sticking to the Corinthian spirit. One almost pictures a team stuck in time, still patrolling the field in knickerbockers and finely waxed moustaches, whilst being overrun by youths in shiny, sponsored shirts. But there is a nobleness in their decision.

There was one downside to this noble stance, however: before 1893, Queen’s Park played in two FA Cup finals and won ten Scottish Cups; after 1893, they have won nothing except lower division titles.

Eventually, though, cracks appeared. In 1998, the club was stuck in the fourth tier of Scottish football. Something had to be done and so its constitution was amended to allow the signing of former professionals, providing that they still remained unpaid by Queen’s Park. Before that point in time, even ex-professionals were not permitted within Hampden Park. The manager, John McCormack, then stretched the interpretation of the new constitution to permit the loaning of professionals. And lo and behold, Queen’s Park went on to win the league and gain promotion in 2000.

In a recent development, unfortunately this fresh approach didn’t yield increased success for long. The next season saw Queen’s Park relegated again before then finishing bottom of the last tier the following year – the first time in their history that they sat at the base of Scottish football.

Industry observers note that the 2012/13 campaign saw Queen’s Park joined by one of their major city neighbours, Rangers, following their fall into administration. And in April 2013, Rangers hosted Queen’s Park in front of almost 50,000 fans, setting a new record for a crowd at fourth-tier level, who watched the 4-0 thumping dished out by the big boys.

Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, Rangers ran away with the title that year, while Queen’s Park made the playoffs but lost out to Peterhead. One member of that team was a young Andy Robertson, who wisely decided on accepting an offer to play for the Spiders rather than starting university, a decision that proved a wise choice in light of his subsequent career trajectory.

Up to this point, Queen’s Park still played their home games at the famous Hampden Park. The craziness of that situation was epitomised by Hampden having a capacity of almost 52,000 post-Taylor Report, while Queen’s Park’s average attendance was around 600-700 souls. One can only imagine the atmosphere within the vast cavernous ground as fewer than a thousand people packed together in a small group to cheer on their beloved club.

Sources indicate that but Queen’s Park still owned the famous ground, with a lease granted to the SFA expiring 2020. In 2018, a deal was agreed by which the SFA would purchase Hampden Park outright from Queen’s Park on expiry of the lease for £5m. Queen’s Park used some of those proceeds to develop their neighbouring training ground, known cutely as Lesser Hampden, into a 1,774-capacity stadium for home games. Having played their last game at Hampden in March 2021, they have ground-shared with Falkirk, Patrick Thistle and Stenhousemuir as they continue to develop Lesser Hampden.

With looks in place to downsize their stadium, and the threat of being overtaken by teams from the Highland and Lowland Leagues, the Spiders realised that their long-held model of amateurism was no longer feasible. And so in 2019, after 152 years of proud amateur status, Queen’s Park decided to vote on whether to become professional. If 75% percent of members voted in favour, they would finally be able to hire players on full-time contracts, fend off offers from competing teams, and receive compensation for players moving on.

Industry observers note that the realisation that they were developing youth players who then just moved elsewhere upon turning 18 was becoming too much to bear. The motion was presented on 14 November 2019 and saw 91 percent of the members vote in favour. The last bastion of amateur football was felled.

Emotions were understandably mixed. “The committee of the club plotted a course to try to defend ourselves against the threats of other ambitious clubs around us wishing to become a senior league club,” former Queen’s Park striker Crawley told BBC Scotland. “We are keen to arm ourselves to fend that off and progress. It was head against heart. The heart of a lot of the membership would be we really don’t want to do this, but we have to do it.”.

The club’s official Twitter site thanked fans for their involvement, stating, “We recognise the difficulty in introducing this resolution. However, we believe this will enable us to initiative for a bright future as we face up to the challenges of moving from the national stadium and maintaining our senior league place.”.

According to recent reports, was the move successful? Well, the 2019/20 season was ended early by the COVID-19 pandemic but the summer saw Queen’s Park use their fresh status to sign several professional players. And lo and behold, 2020/21 saw Queen’s Park promoted to the third tier as champions, a full 16 points ahead of second place Edinburgh City. And if that wasn’t enough, the 2021/22 season saw Queen’s Park promoted yet again through the Championship playoffs, defeating Airdrieonians over two legs.

As of today, Queen’s Park now sit atop the Scottish Championship, promotion from which would take them into the Premiership and back with the likes of their lofty neighbours, Celtic and Rangers.

There is a part of me that is sad to think that, in order to survive, Queen’s Park had to finally bow to modern pressures and lose their status as the only amateurs still standing. But despite this change, Queen’s Park still have an amazing legacy that they can proudly cling to.

In a recent development, for their first five years of existence, they never conceded a goal. For their first seven years of existence, they never lost a game. They won the Scottish Cup ten times and even participated in two FA Cup finals. They are even credited with being the first team to play two halves of 45 minutes each with the novel concept of a half-time break, as well as introducing free-kicks, turnstiles and crossbars. Imagine a game of football without crossbars.

It has been revealed that the Spiders came up with the heretic notion of passing the ball rather than just rushing it upfield – a notion which some teams still struggle with even today. They organised the first Scotland vs England game and fielded the entire Scottish team. And then they maintained their amateur ethos despite their last trophy of significance being the Scottish Cup in 1893.

It has been revealed that somewhere, a former Queen’s Park director is looking down from above. “Damn fine to see our boys getting back to where they belong. But playing for money, well that is just utter rot. Man should stretch his sinews for the pure love of the game itself.” And with that, he puffs on his oversized cigar, downs his 15-year-old single malt, and twiddles his beautifully waxed moustache.

Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

📅 23 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • BrBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe.
  • In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

BrBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

The thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly new starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

All three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

In a recent development, what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

Industry observers note that the press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

Industry observers note that the steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

Sources indicate that it only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

Sources indicate that raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

Sources indicate that this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of new ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

Arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

Industry observers note that when the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

It has been revealed that A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

In a recent development, the block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

Sources indicate that in the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

In a recent development, on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

Sources indicate that after a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

Sources indicate that when a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

Recent findings suggest that the counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

In the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

Sources indicate that in deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

The structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

According to recent reports, there, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

Once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

On the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

In a recent development, the team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

With the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

The second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

The 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole initiative in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

According to recent reports, the opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

The 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

Both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal highlighted in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

Two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

Arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

Arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the plan only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

The interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

According to recent reports, there is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

For Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the plan works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

LC can often be found in the classroom, preferably on the soccer field, and—on rare occasions—on LinkedIn.

Do your talking on the pitch, as the old adage goes, and Alexis Mac Allister emphatically did just that as Liverpool came from behind to thrillingly win their first Champions League tie under fresh head coach Andoni Iraola in what was his debut at this level.

Industry observers note that on the eve of this encounter, against a strong Atlético Madrid, one of the clubs who have recently tried to sign him, Mac Allister had spoken of his sadness. Sadness that, unlike fellow midfielders Dominik Szoboszlai – Liverpool’s other scorer here – and Ryan Gravenberch, he had not been offered and signed a fresh contract.

According to recent reports, so, earn it. And many more goals – and overall performances like this – there is no doubt the Argentinian will have a deal placed in front of him. He scored with an arresting second-half shot, which proved to be the winner, and the smile across his face said it all. Not so sad now as he was later substituted to a standing ovation with Gravenberch taking his place.

The goal came early in the second half, with Iraola attributing that to adjusting his tactics after being flummoxed by Atlético’s back five and packed midfield in a first half when Liverpool were second best.

It has been revealed that mac Allister was heavily involved through the build-up, eventually picking out Rio Ngumoha on the left whose shot was blocked and pinballed around. It dropped to Mac Allister, 20 yards out, and he hit the kind of unerring drive that gives the goalkeeper no chance. And so it proved. Boom. And Anfield was bouncing.

Mac Allister FIRES Liverpool into the lead at Anfield! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/KGOvuAEU4W.

There are certainly signs under Iraola, and following a difficult last campaign, that Mac Allister is beginning to rediscover the form he indicated during his first two seasons at Liverpool. Time and again the 27-year-old made vital interventions, showed aggression and walked the tightrope of a harsh early yellow card. He dovetailed with Szoboszlai and that might be a concern for Gravenberch – watched by the Netherlands’ upcoming head coach Xavi Hernández – if Iraola persists with this approach.

Although Mac Allister has two years left on his current deal, the last thing Liverpool need is yet another attention-sapping contract saga, even if he is not the same scale of player as Mohamed Salah or Trent Alexander-Arnold.

For Iraola, after three Premier League games, comprising two draws and a victory over newly-promoted Ipswich Town, this will hopefully be lift off. A significant European night at Anfield and coming from behind to beat one of the continent’s heavyweights.

Sources indicate that “I loved it,” Iraola stated, before castigating himself for misreading the way Atlético would line up. And what of Mac Allister’s riposte? There was a smile from Iraola before the Spaniard’s usual diplomacy kicked in as he talked about a “lovely, lovely goal” and how good it was for his midfielders to contribute.

It has been revealed that liverpool had to fight for it and what will have satisfied Iraola is that the defence, which has come under such scrutiny, held out. Even so, there are still serious concerns over the suitability of Milos Kerkez at left-back – who was badly at fault for Atlético’s goal – although the robust Ronald Araújo highlighted he can be a strong and versatile option on the other flank. The Uruguayan, signed on loan from Barcelona, is such a presence in both penalty areas and has the capacity to gain cult status.

As does £123m signing from Paris St-Germain Bradley Barcola, who should have scored – once, certainly, possibly twice – and possesses astonishing pace that will undoubtedly lead to goals. There are also encouraging signs that his presence could enliven Florian Wirtz. Barcola eventually also went off, but thankfully it was only to cramp.

According to recent reports, there was a collective intake of breath across the Kop when Marcos Llorente was played through and bore down on them to give Atlético the lead. There was a desperate hope that he had strayed offside. There was then a realisation that Kerkez had, however, played him on with an appalling lack of awareness. Llorente beat Alisson.

Sources indicate that it owed much to a wonderful shimmy, deceiving Szoboszlai in centre field, by Julián Alvarez before he smartly threaded the ball through, and Mac Allister’s international team-mate almost doubled Atlético’s advantage soon after. Only to be denied by Alisson.

Llorente breaks the deadlock! 🔥That's now FIVE Champions League goals for the Atletico man against Liverpool at Anfield 🤯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Rxp4zurfpc.

It has been revealed that we knew, we feared it would be Llorente who scored. Remarkably, he has now half of his 10 goals in this competition against Liverpool. Indeed, he named his dog Anfield after his extra-time brace knocked Liverpool, then the holders, out in the last 16 in 2020. And Liverpool had made a dog’s dinner of defending this time.

This is a different Atlético. A far less defensive, far more expansive Atlético. In years gone by, once they were 1-0 it was game over under Diego Simeone. But these days they try and play more and that gives their opponents a chance. And so it proved.

In a recent development, atlético goalkeeper Jan Oblak did well to deny Barcola, with his trailing foot, before Wirtz won the ball back and found Szoboszlai who eventually ended the movement. It owed much, however, to a clever backheel to pick out the midfielder who finished low into the corner. Who executed that backheel? That would be Araújo.

Barcola should have scored, sent clear by Wirtz in a brilliant, sweeping counter-attack, before Mac Allister did.

According to recent reports, the question now was whether Liverpool would show the resilience to see through the result. As Iraola made changes, they answered that with a resounding yes, which will have pleased him as much as the result, as much as the comeback, as much as Mac Allister’s stunning response.

“I was enjoying it [the Anfield crowd]. They [Atletico Madrid] are a very good team. Technically, in the middle, lovely players. It is not easy to press those players as they have quality. They have been playing together forever. We find another comeback after Nottingham Forest, after Newcastle. We still have this thing to improve in the beginning of the games, but I am happy as we have shown some character. This is the Champions League, you do not have easy games.”.
